title: Uluru and the Outback
objective: After this level you can describe the Outback and what Uluru means to Aboriginal Australians.
summary: Uluru rises 348 m from the Outback plain, the tip of a much bigger buried slab, red with rusting iron. It is sacred to the Anangu, who own it; the climb closed in 2019.

cards.headline: A rock in the Outback is taller than the Eiffel Tower. That's just the tip.
cards.body: Most of it is hidden underground. And the part you can see has been sacred to the people who own it for tens of thousands of years.

cards.headline: A buried giant
cards.body: Level 81's dry, flat, nearly empty interior is the Outback. In the Outback of the Northern Territory, one rock rises 348 m above the surrounding plain: Uluru. That's taller than the Eiffel Tower. Yet Uluru and its neighbor Kata Tjuta are only the tips of huge rock slabs that carry on underground for up to 6 km. You're looking at the top of a buried giant.

cards.headline: A rock that rusts
cards.body: Uluru is made of arkose, a kind of sandstone with iron in it. Over time that iron rusts, just like an old bike left out in the rain, and the rust is Uluru's famous red. In grey patches you can see the rock's original color. So the most famous red rock in Australia is, underneath, a grey one wearing a coat of rust.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: the red isn't sand or paint. It's rust, with grey rock underneath.

cards.headline: Whose rock?
cards.body: Uluru belongs to the Aṉangu, its Traditional Owners. It has been sacred to them for tens of thousands of years, and under Tjukurpa, Aṉangu law and culture, climbing it was generally not allowed. In 1985 the park was handed back to Aṉangu, who lease it to the Australian Government and run it jointly with Parks Australia. On 26 October 2019 the climb closed for good. Visitors now admire Uluru the way its owners always asked: from the ground.

cards.headline: Uluru: understood
learned: Uluru rises 348 m, taller than the Eiffel Tower
It's the tip of a slab reaching up to 6 km down
Its red is rust; its original color is grey
Sacred to the Aṉangu, who own it; the climb closed in 2019

questions.prompt: What gives Uluru its famous red color?

options.label: Red desert sand blown onto it
options.rationale: The red is in the rock itself, not dust on top.

options.label: Paint from ancient rock art
options.rationale: The whole surface is red, far beyond any art.

options.label: Light from the setting Sun
options.rationale: The rock stays red all day.

questions.explanation: Uluru's arkose contains iron. The iron rusts, and the rust makes the red; the rock's original color is grey.

questions.prompt: Why was the climb up Uluru closed?

options.label: The rock was cracking apart
options.rationale: The reason was cultural, not geological.

options.label: Climbing it goes against Aṉangu law, and Aṉangu own the park
The government bought the land from Aṉangu
options.rationale: It's the reverse: the park was handed back to Aṉangu in 1985.

options.label: Tourists stopped visiting the Outback
options.rationale: Visitors still come; they just don't climb.

questions.explanation: Uluru is sacred to its Aṉangu owners, and climbing it was not generally allowed under Tjukurpa. The climb closed in 2019.

questions.prompt: From Level 7: Uluru rises 348 m above the plain around it. Why isn't that the height a map would give?

options.label: Map heights include the rock hidden underground
options.rationale: Maps measure up from a zero line, not down into buried rock.

options.label: Maps give heights only for mountains
options.rationale: Any point can have a height; the question is where zero sits.

options.label: Map heights usually start from sea level
Map heights start from Earth's center
options.rationale: The usual zero is mean sea level.

questions.explanation: A map height is usually measured above mean sea level, while Uluru's 348 m is measured from the plain around it.
